# Answer key - Chapter 10: Logging and log integrity {.unnumbered}

<!-- Source-only: this directory is excluded from the render in _quarto.yml
     ("!answers/"). Never link these files from a chapter. Numbering must
     match the chapter's Self-check section 1:1. -->

**Q1** *(tests @sec-10-logs-events · basic)* - **Correct: b.**
This is the Guidance's separation as the chapter gives it (CSA, 2024,
p. 125): logs are complete, detailed, persistent but batched and delayed;
events record a change, arrive within seconds and are not retained unless
saved - which is why events can trigger real-time alerts; a and d reverse
the two, c denies the separation.

**Q2** *(tests @sec-10-logs-events · basic)* - **Correct: c.**
Resource Logs are not collected by default; a diagnostic setting must first
be enabled or an agent installed, "and this gap commonly leaves exactly the
logs one wants missing when they are needed"; a describes the Activity
Log's retention, b and d are invented.

**Q3** *(tests @sec-10-log-sources · basic)* - **Accepted answers:**
"to know what each source captures and to make sure the security-relevant
sources are actually recorded"; "because an event that was never logged
cannot be investigated" (any phrasing with both halves: know the sources,
ensure they are recorded, since unlogged events cannot be investigated).

**Q4** *(tests @sec-10-logs-events · basic)* - **Accepted answers:**
"who (source address or caller), what (the request or operation), when (the
timestamp) and the outcome (200, 403 or Succeeded)" (any phrasing naming
who, what, when and outcome/result).

**Q5** *(tests @sec-10-central-collection · basic)* - **Correct: b.**
The cascading log architecture (CSA, 2024, p. 134): each environment sends
to one central store, the security-relevant subset is filtered into a
separate, well-protected audit environment kept long-term, and from there
the logs feed the SIEM; a, c and d contradict the cascade.

**Q6** *(tests @sec-10-log-integrity · basic)* - **Correct: a.**
These are the chapter's three measures: off-host shipping as logs are
produced, append-only/write-once storage, and restricted access under the
least-privilege rules of Session 7; b, c and d each leave the record under
the attacker's control or delay its escape from the host (a safeguard under
the attacker's control is no safeguard).

**Q7 - applied scenario** *(tests @sec-10-exercises · applied)* -
**Model answer:** The team relies on the copies in the central,
append-only log store: the Nginx access log, the system journal, Nextcloud's
access and audit logs and the firewall's records, all forwarded off-host
as they were written (@def-logagg, @exm-logship-trc), plus the management
plane logs (on Azure, the Activity Log), which the attacker on the VM never
controlled. Those copies are beyond doubt because (1) they left the host in
real time, before the attacker could act on them, (2) the store is
append-only or write-once, so even someone with access could add but not
edit or delete, and (3) access to the store is restricted under least
privilege - together this is log integrity (@def-logintegrity), and the
documented preservation of the evidence is the chain of custody that lets
the timeline stand before a regulator. The copies still on the VM prove
nothing because the attacker had full control of the host for weeks and
could rewrite the record freely: a timeline assembled from records that
might have been tampered with proves nothing. **Grading notes:** full
credit requires naming the off-host central copies (including a
management-plane source), all three integrity measures, chain of custody by
name, and the tampering argument against the on-host copies; partial credit
for three of these four elements.

## Sketch answers to the chapter exercises

(1) *(@exr-10-two-roles-of-logs - The two roles of logs)*
Operational: understanding the system and reconstructing behaviour, for
example the Nginx access log or the system journal. Evidential: the timeline
and proof of who did what during an incident, for example Nextcloud's audit
log and the management plane logs.

(2) *(@exr-10-ephemeral-hosts - Central collection for ephemeral hosts)*
Ephemeral instances disappear with
demand, taking locally stored logs with them; forwarding logs to a central
store as they are written preserves them beyond the life of the host.

(3) *(@exr-10-log-integrity-cia - Log integrity and the CIA triad)*
Log integrity is the integrity property of CIA applied to the audit
record, the assurance that it has not been altered or deleted. Logs kept only
on the host fail it because an attacker who controls the host can edit or
wipe them, destroying the record of their own actions.

(4) *(@exr-10-protecting-log-integrity - Protecting log integrity)*
Ship logs off-host
as they are produced; store them append-only or write-once; restrict who may
access the log store (least privilege). Central collection is an integrity
control because logs that left the host immediately are beyond the reach of
the host's attacker.

(5) *(@exr-10-chain-of-custody - Chain of custody)*
Chain of custody is the documented preservation of
evidence so that its integrity can be demonstrated later (to management,
regulators or a court); off-host, append-only logs provide a trustworthy,
untampered record, which is what lets the attack timeline in Session 12's
Detection and Analysis phase stand as proof.
